Last week I was in Dublin for the 13th International Congress on Environmental Modelling and Software (iEMSs). This was my second time at this conference, having first attended in 2022, and it has stayed one of my favourite communities: people who build models to support environmental decisions and who are just as happy to talk about the software underneath them as about the results.

This time I convened a session together with [Orlando Roman](https://im.ibi.ethz.ch/en/people/scientific-assistants/orlando-roman-garcia.html) and [Richard Hewitt](https://www.linkedin.com/in/richard-hewitt-09408937/): *Synthesising advances in uncertainty exploration in land change modelling to inform planning and policy*. Reviews of land use and land cover change (LULCC) modelling have for years called for more attention to the various sources of uncertainty in the modelling process. Much of the work that followed has been consolidative, aimed at reducing uncertainty to improve model performance. That matters, but it leaves a gap.

Our aim with the session was to widen the frame and treat uncertainty as an opportunity rather than a limitation: something to explore in support of more robust and adaptive decisions. We invited contributions from across the spectrum of modelling approaches, whether process-based, pattern-based or agent-based, and across different forms of uncertainty, from parameters and model structure through to input data and future scenarios. The common thread we were looking for was how the effects of uncertainty on model outputs can be communicated as something planners and policymakers can actually act on.

Within the session I gave a presentation on behalf of Orlando: [Discovering decision-relevant scenarios in large ensembles of Land Use and Cover Change projections](../presentations/2026_07_15_iemss.qmd). It covers our work using large ensembles to explore uncertainty in LULCC scenarios and to find the boundaries at which scenarios start to differ in ways that matter for planning.

I also gave a workshop with Isabel Nicholson Thomas and Manuel Kurmann on using Quarto across the whole research workflow: [One Tool to Rule Them All: Quarto for Documentation, Presentations, Manuscripts and Outreach](https://iat-dml.github.io/quarto-workshop/). We prepared it as part of the DML group's work, and it covers research diaries, manuscripts, slides, websites and dashboards, all rendered from the same plain text sources. The site is built to be followed on your own afterwards, so it works as a reference as much as a live session.

If there is enough interest from the session contributors, we would like to take the discussion further as a collective review or position paper on exploratory uncertainty analysis in LULCC modelling. If that sounds like your area of work, please do get in touch.
